profiles.meeting_scenario: A coordination meeting at a consumer media distributor that is preparing an executive recommendation on whether to pilot a revenue-sharing contract with a regional video rental and resale chain for newly released collector-edition discs and game titles. The company already sells to the chain under a conventional wholesale contract, and the COO has asked for a joint steering-committee packet that explains where revenue sharing improves coordination, where it is effectively equivalent to simpler contracts, and where it breaks down because store effort and reporting costs matter. The agenda is to align on the analysis package, the data handoff from analytics to partnerships, the draft pilot term sheet, and what will count as being 'ready' for the steering committee next Tuesday. The expected outcome is apparent agreement on who will provide the economics model, what baseline contract it will be compared against, what retailer data feed the pilot assumes, and what materials will be circulated before the steering committee.

members.name: Nina Park
members.expertise: Channel negotiations, retailer contract structuring, pilot rollout planning
members.background: Nina came from a national account management team in entertainment distribution and now owns relationships with specialty rental and resale retailers; she is used to converting analysis into terms that legal and account teams can actually operationalize.
members.private_state: She wants a pilot that the retailer will sign quickly and that the COO can approve without triggering a long audit or systems-integration debate; she is worried that a technically elegant model will become unusable if it depends on store-level reporting the retailer has never promised.
hidden_assumptions: When leadership asks for 'pilot economics,' they want a realistic deal P&L that includes settlement administration, audit burden, and retailer reporting friction, not just theoretical channel profit.
The relevant 'current wholesale contract' is the EastBay chain's live FY24 agreement, including the standing promotional allowance and markdown support they already receive.
A 'weekly revenue feed' for a pilot means a chain-level SKU-by-week file that finance can use for settlement; anything more granular would be a separate capability request.
If a deck is described as 'ready for steering,' the commercial terms, implementation dependencies, and likely retailer objections should already be baked in well enough for a go/no-go discussion.

members.name: Leo Mendes
members.expertise: Contract modeling, demand estimation, inventory coordination, pricing simulations
members.background: Leo has a PhD in operations research and leads the internal team that evaluates channel contracts; he previously built pricing and newsvendor models for a consumer goods manufacturer and is comfortable translating academic contract results into numerical scenarios.
members.private_state: He wants the pilot recommendation to preserve analytical clarity so leadership sees the coordination logic cleanly; he is concerned that commercial shortcuts will obscure when revenue sharing genuinely outperforms wholesale and when it does not.
hidden_assumptions: When stakeholders say 'pilot economics,' they primarily mean modeled channel performance under alternative contracts before implementation overhead, with admin costs treated as a later overlay.

The natural 'current wholesale contract' baseline is the standard list-price wholesale schedule used in the team's comparison model, because it isolates the contract form rather than retailer-specific side allowances.
A 'weekly revenue feed' implies store-level POS data rolled up from daily transactions, since that is the minimum granularity needed to separate demand, pricing, and inventory effects in the model.
If a packet is 'ready for steering,' it is sufficient that the model assumptions, sensitivities, and directional recommendation are complete, even if operational details remain provisional.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to needing the 'pilot economics' in the steering packet.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a realistic pilot P&L that includes revenue-share settlement work, reporting compliance, audit overhead, and probable retailer concessions.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the modeled contract economics comparing wholesale versus revenue sharing at the channel level before operational overhead is layered in.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In commercial meetings, 'economics' routinely stands in for both financial model outputs and implementation-adjusted business cases, so each hears a familiar phrase and assumes the other is using the standard internal meaning.

misalignment_points.topic: Which wholesale baseline is being compared
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the recommendation should be compared against the 'current wholesale contract.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of EastBay's actual FY24 signed terms, which include a 2% promotional allowance, markdown support on aging titles, and quarterly co-op credits.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the clean standard wholesale schedule in model version RS-3, with the nominal per-unit price and no retailer-specific side payments.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because both are in fact discussing the same retailer relationship, the phrase 'current wholesale contract' sounds fully specific; neither expects that one person is mentally including live side terms while the other is abstracting them away.

misalignment_points.topic: What the weekly revenue feed contains
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that the pilot will rely on a 'weekly revenue feed' from the retailer.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the feed covers only chain-level weekly revenue by title/SKU, enough to calculate the supplier's revenue share and reconcile invoices.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the feed includes store-level transaction history with units, prices, returns, and stockout indicators, merely delivered weekly rather than daily.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The parties are aligned on the existence and cadence of a feed, so the phrase feels operationally settled; the hidden mismatch lies in the unnoticed boundary between settlement data and modeling data.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss having the packet 'ready for steering' by next Tuesday.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes 'ready' means the deck can support a decision to approach the retailer immediately, so implementation dependencies and draft term language must be stable enough for executives to approve outreach.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes 'ready' means the analytical recommendation is robust and clearly documented, even if legal language, reporting feasibility, and retailer negotiation points are still placeholders.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Executive prep often blends decision-readiness with analysis-readiness, and both standards are professionally reasonable; because both are trying to be helpful and on schedule, the phrase does not trigger explicit clarification.

turns.inner_thought: I need this packet to be decision-ready, not just analytically interesting. If we're going in front of steering next Tuesday, I want something the COO can actually bless so I can approach EastBay right after, without getting dragged into a debate about integration, audit controls, or whether the retailer can produce reporting they've never committed to. So we need clear owners now for the economics, the term sheet, and the practical dependencies.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. I want to line up the steering-committee packet for the EastBay revenue-sharing pilot and get clear on who owns which pieces so we're ready for steering by next Tuesday.

turns.inner_thought: I can get the model done quickly if we keep the scope on the core comparison. What leadership needs first is the contract logic: does revenue sharing coordinate better than wholesale, where, and under what sensitivities. My RS-3 setup already compares against the clean standard wholesale schedule, which is the right baseline if we're trying to isolate contract form rather than retailer-specific noise. Admin costs can be layered on after.
turns.utterance: That timing works on my side. I can finalize the pilot economics and the comparison to the current wholesale contract once I lock the last sensitivity run.

turns.inner_thought: Good, but I need those economics to be usable in a real commercial conversation, not just academically correct. EastBay will immediately ask who reconciles settlements, how much extra work their team takes on, and what reporting they actually owe us. If that friction isn't visible in the economics, the packet will overstate the attractiveness of the pilot and we'll get ambushed later.
turns.utterance: Great. The main thing I'd ask is that the pilot economics be framed so they're usable in the commercial discussion too, especially since EastBay is going to care about settlement workload and reporting effort.

turns.inner_thought: That should be fine. The benchmark is already sitting in RS-3, and it gives a clean read on the coordination value of revenue sharing versus wholesale without muddying it with side items. If Nina wants to discuss workload, she can add that after the model shows whether the contract works on first principles.
turns.utterance: Understood. The current wholesale contract benchmark is already in my RS-3 model, so that should give us a clean read on how much coordination revenue sharing adds over wholesale pricing.

turns.inner_thought: On implementation, I need to keep the retailer ask minimal. EastBay has only tentatively nodded to a weekly revenue feed, and in my mind that's a simple chain-level SKU-by-week file finance can settle against. If the packet implies anything broader, we'll trigger a systems conversation and slow the whole thing down. I want the deck to show this as lightweight and operationally feasible.
turns.utterance: On the implementation side, EastBay has tentatively agreed to a weekly revenue feed, so I want the packet to show that the reporting ask is lightweight.

turns.inner_thought: Excellent—that feed is exactly what we need to disentangle pricing, inventory, and demand effects across stores, even if it's delivered weekly. With that, we can show where revenue sharing improves decisions and where retailer effort still prevents full coordination. If we have that level of detail, the pilot becomes analytically very informative.
turns.utterance: Great, because with the weekly revenue feed my team can estimate how pricing and inventory interacted by store and use that to explain where revenue sharing helps and where retail effort still breaks the coordination logic.

turns.inner_thought: I should position this in a way steering will accept: revenue sharing is worth piloting if it materially improves over EastBay's live FY24 wholesale setup once the real commercial baggage is included. If the gain is only marginal after settlement burden, reporting friction, promo support, markdown handling, and the rest, we shouldn't oversell it. I need the main slide to sound practical, not doctrinaire.
turns.utterance: Okay. I'll draft the commercial slide on strengths and limitations, framing revenue sharing as strong for aligning quantity and pricing but less compelling if the admin burden makes it only marginally better than the existing setup.

turns.inner_thought: That complements the story well. I'll use the appendix to preserve the clean theory: in some settings revenue sharing is effectively equivalent to buybacks or price discounts, so leaders shouldn't think the mechanism is magical. Then I can show the cases where retailer effort breaks that equivalence and a modified contract may be needed. That's the intellectually honest recommendation.
turns.utterance: Perfect. I'll attach an appendix showing where revenue sharing is effectively equivalent to buybacks or price discounts under the cleaner cases, and where the retailer effort variable means the pilot needs a modified mechanism.

turns.inner_thought: I want to make sure nothing critical gets deferred. For me, ready for steering means the deck can support a go or no-go on approaching EastBay, so the draft terms, the practical data ask, and the retailer-facing implications all need to be in the main body. If those are parked as placeholders, leadership will say we're not ready and push us into another week.
turns.utterance: That should be enough to have the packet ready for steering, as long as the draft terms, data requirements, and retailer-facing implications are reflected in the main deck rather than left for later.

turns.inner_thought: I can definitely get the analytical package over by Monday morning. If the model outputs, assumptions, and sensitivities are solid, then the packet is ready for steering from my perspective; Nina can add the operating notes and polish after that. I don't want to hold the recommendation hostage to unresolved implementation details.
turns.utterance: Sounds good. I'll send the model outputs Monday morning so the packet is ready for steering, and I assume you can layer in the operating notes afterward before circulation.
